books.section: Topic 8.6 Early Steps in the Civil Rights Movement (1940s and 1950s)

options.text: Renewed legal challenges to segregation and civil rights momentum

options.misconception: Brown desegregated all public schools immediately.
options.text: The immediate desegregation of all public schools without resistance

options.misconception: Brown led to the repeal of the Fourteenth Amendment.
options.text: The repeal of the Fourteenth Amendment

options.misconception: Brown ended federal involvement in education.
options.text: The end of federal involvement in education

rationales.A: Brown energized legal challenges and gave the civil rights movement a major precedent, even though implementation was slow and resisted.
rationales.B: Resistance was intense; desegregation was not immediate.
rationales.C: The Fourteenth Amendment was the basis for Brown; it was not repealed.
rationales.D: Federal involvement in education grew; it did not end.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what a Supreme Court precedent does. It gives later challenges a legal foundation.
2. Name the effect. Brown energized legal challenges and gave the movement momentum.
3. Test the overstatements. Desegregation was slow and resisted, the Fourteenth Amendment stands, and federal involvement grew.
4. Keep the effect honest. A precedent matters even when implementation lags.
Remember: a ruling's contribution can be momentum, not instant change.

stimulus.source_note: Brown v. Board of Education, 1954, unanimous opinion by Chief Justice Earl Warren, public domain. Photograph: Thomas J. O’Halloran, 1955, Library of Congress.
stimulus.text: “Segregation of white and colored children in public schools has a detrimental effect upon the colored children. The impact is greater when it has the sanction of the law . . . Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.”
